And then, through the worked-thin air, a familiar warmth finds you, and for one window the size of a held breath it is just Gin — lucid, horrified, reaching back across the seam not to pull you through but to push you away, his cold passenger asleep or distracted or simply outvoted for one human second. You shouldn't be this bright, he tells you, in the only language the wall leaves him, and you understand it is both the most loving and the most frightened thing your brother has ever said to you. You have found him. He has found you. And the finding, done this brightly, this close to the seat, has put you both exactly where the Healer would most like you to be: in the same place, lit, legible, and reachable through each other.

choices.x: Reach back to Gin through the window — answer him while it's open.
choices.hint: One true exchange with your brother, mind to mind, might give you the seam from the inside and a thread of him to hold. It is also the brightest possible flare fired directly at the wall, in full view of the seat that just opened its eye, using the one channel the Healer most wants mapped.

choices.x: Damp yourself down — fold the registers, go dark at the wall.
choices.hint: Go quiet now and you may slip the Axis's attention before it fixes on you. Folding shut here means losing the window with Gin, perhaps the last lucid one, and walking blind back into a city you can no longer fully read.

choices.x: Step toward the wall while it's thin and you're bright enough to cross.
choices.hint: Brightness this close to a worked membrane might be enough to step through and reach Gin in the flesh. Crossing a thinned wall toward the empty seat is exactly the motion the Healer engineered the whole membrane to invite — you would be walking, lit, into the trap as its final piece.

look.title: The Long Walk
acts: Open: the city decides for you
Deepen: what the short ways step over
Converge: arriving without a faction at your back

beats.scene: The kitchen, 3:47 on the stove clock, and the decision to take nothing but your feet
prose: There are five ways out of this room and four of them ask you to spend something you can't get back — a name handed to a badge, a favour owed to the Grid, the registers behind your eyes pried open until the world goes thin around you. You stand in the cooling kitchen with the rice still warm in the cooker and you understand, with the flat certainty that arrives only at four in the morning, that you are going to refuse all four. You are going to do the slow, stupid, human thing. You are going to walk out the door with nothing in your hands and look for your brother the way a person looks for a person.

It is not nobility. You want to be honest with yourself about that much while you still can be. It is fear — fear of the badge, which keeps what it touches; fear of the Gift, which keeps the one who uses it; fear most of all of becoming, in the search for Gin, the kind of thing Gin would no longer recognise as his sibling. The other roads are faster and you can feel the speed of them pulling at you like a draft under the door. But fast is how he was taken. Fast is the seam in the air at chest height where something stepped through that should not be able to step through anything. You decide, in the dark, that whatever has him moves at the speed of taking, and you will move at the speed of finding, and you will trust that the second speed reaches further in the end.

So you do the small things a person does. You write a note for the family that says less than you know. You put on shoes that can take a night of pavement. You leave the rice. And at the genkan you stop with your hand on the door and feel the absence of everything the other roads would have armed you with — no procedure, no protection, no sight — and you step out into the Obon dark anyway, into a Tokyo lit for the returning dead, with nothing to find your living brother but attention and time.

choices.x: Leave now, in the dark, before you can talk yourself onto a faster road.
choices.hint: Move while the trail is warm and you'll be on the streets ahead of the dawn crowds. You also leave with no money plan, no contact, and no idea how many nights this costs — the long walk has no timetable, and Gin's lucid windows do.

choices.x: Wait for first light and gather what a traveller needs — cash, a map, his photo.
choices.hint: An hour of preparation makes the walk survivable for days instead of one. Every hour you spend packing is an hour the thing wearing your brother spends walking him north.

choices.x: Knock on one door first — wake someone who loved Gin and ask before the city wakes.
choices.hint: A second pair of eyes and a second memory could halve the search. It also means letting another person into a danger you chose to face alone precisely so no one else would have to.

beats.scene: The last trains gone, the night city of Obon, choosing a direction by ordinary signs
prose: Without the sight you have no line of cooling footprints to follow, and at first the loss of it is vertiginous — you keep reaching for a sense you've decided not to use, the way a tongue keeps finding the gap of a pulled tooth. But the city is not silent to ordinary eyes; it is only quieter, and slower, and you have to learn its plainer language fast. A man your brother's height was seen, or wasn't. A timetable on the kitchen shelf was folded back to the Kita line. A cab driver at the Sugamo rank remembers a fare who didn't speak and didn't seem to know where he was going, only north, always a little further north, as if north were a person calling him.

This is the road's whole discipline and you feel it close around you like a habit: you cannot leap, so you must accumulate. Each scrap is nearly nothing — a direction, a time, the colour of a coat — and only by laying them end to end across a night of walking do they become a thread you can pull. You walk Hakusan-dori with the lanterns swinging overhead, the families home for Obon eating late, the smell of grilling and incense and rain that hasn't fallen yet, and you do the arithmetic of the ordinary: who would have been awake, who would have seen, who would tell a stranger the truth at this hour. The dead are supposedly walking these same streets tonight, come home for the festival. You find you are not afraid of them. You are afraid of being too slow for the one who isn't dead yet.

By the third hour your feet have begun to hurt in the specific, instructive way that tells you this is real now, this is your body spent on this and not retrievable, and somewhere under the tiredness you notice the first quiet gift of the slow road: you are still entirely yourself. No register has opened. Nothing on the other side of anything has turned to look at you. You are just a tired person walking north through a festival, asking after a brother, and for one block the ordinariness feels less like weakness than like the only armour that was ever going to work.

choices.x: Follow the cab driver's 'north' literally — straight up the Kita line on foot.
choices.hint: The driver's instinct points the same way the timetable does; trusting it could save you a night. It also stakes everything on one half-asleep memory, and if he's wrong you've walked hours into the wrong ward.

choices.x: Work the witnesses outward in a slow spiral instead of chasing one lead.
choices.hint: Methodical canvassing catches the contradictions a single lead would hide. It is achingly slow, and the trail cools a degree with every door, every dawn, every hour you spend being thorough.

choices.x: Stop walking and just watch one intersection he'd have to cross.
choices.hint: Patience at a chokepoint sometimes beats motion — let the city bring him to you. Or let the whole night pass at one corner while he takes a street you never imagined, and learn nothing but the look of a lamppost at four a.m.

beats.scene: A convenience store at the edge of nowhere, the small economy of asking strangers for help
prose: There is a particular kind of person awake at this hour in a konbini at the edge of a residential ward — the night clerk who has seen everything and judges none of it, the salaryman drinking canned coffee to delay going home, the old woman buying flowers for a grave she'll visit at dawn. You come in under the white light smelling of rain and roads and you have to decide, fast, how much of the truth a stranger will hold for you. Too little and they shrug; too much and they back away from the kind of trouble that follows a sibling looking for a sibling at four in the morning during the festival of the dead. The slow road runs on these small transactions, and you are learning their exchange rate the hard way.

The clerk is younger than you expected and he looks at the photo of Gin a long time before he says anything, and when he speaks it is not what you wanted but it is true, which on this road is the only currency that compounds. He's seen the man. Not tonight — two nights ago, and again last week, the same man, always northbound, always with the slightly wrong walk of someone being steered, and once with a second person who the clerk can't quite describe, except that being near them made the cold drinks case hum in a way he'd reported to maintenance twice. You stand in the fluorescent hum and feel the braid of it: your brother, more than once, on a route, with a passenger the ordinary eye can only register as a malfunction. The slow road has just told you something no faster road would have stopped to hear — that this isn't a kidnapping, it's a routine.

You buy something you don't need, because that is how this economy works, and the clerk tells you one more thing while he makes change: there's a woman who runs a late stall three stations up who 'keeps track of the ones who wander', who the unregistered and the half-touched go to when the official world has no slot for them. He doesn't have a name for what she does. You do — or you have a guess, and the guess is the first time tonight the supernatural has reached into your human search, not as a power you wield but as a place you might walk to. You thank him properly, the way you'd want a stranger thanked for helping look for your brother, and you go back out into the dark with one more thread and the strange warmth of having been, for two minutes, simply helped.

choices.x: Go straight to the woman who 'keeps track of the ones who wander'.
choices.hint: She may have seen Gin's route with eyes that understand it — the best lead of the night. People who track the wandering are rarely free with what they know, and you have nothing to trade but a story she's heard a hundred times.

choices.x: Press the clerk for the route's other stops before you lose him to his shift.
choices.hint: Pinning the whole pattern now means you can find Gin even if the woman won't help. It also keeps a kind young man longer in a conversation that could mark him, to whatever hums the drinks case, as someone who talked.

choices.x: Rest an hour here, eat, let your body keep up with the road.
choices.hint: You cannot walk to Kita on an empty body and a sleepless night; the road is long and you are the vehicle. Every hour of rest is an hour the routine runs without you watching it.

beats.scene: The late stall three stations north, and the people the factions never count
prose: The woman's stall is the kind of place the official world draws no line around — a few stools, a kerosene heater for a night that isn't cold, a hand-lettered menu, and a clientele that the Directorate's registries and the Tower's records have simply never managed to contain. These are the unregistered and the half-touched, the animal-mediums and the once-possessed and the people who saw something once and have organised their whole quiet lives around never seeing it again. They are exactly the people the fast roads step over, because a faction's eye slides off anyone it can't file, and you understand as you sit down among them that the slow road has brought you to the one census that might actually have your brother in it.

The woman does not perform mystery; she ladles soup and watches you decide whether to be honest. When you put Gin's photo on the counter she doesn't touch it, only looks, and then she looks at you — at your eyes, specifically, at the place behind them you have kept folded shut all night — and something in her face settles, as if she has just confirmed a suspicion she'd rather have been wrong about. 'You're his,' she says. 'The one who could look and won't.' It is not a question and it is not an accusation, but it lands like both, and around you the quiet clientele go a degree quieter, the way a room does when someone says the true thing out loud. She has seen Gin. She has seen, she tells you, what walks in his steps. And she has been counting how many of her people have gone north and not come back, the way you count anything you can't stop.

What she gives you is not a location but a shape, and it is worse for being a shape: the northbound ones, the wanderers, the half-touched who drift up the Kita line and thin out of her count — they aren't being taken at random. They're being gathered. Someone up there has been, in her flat word, 'tidying' — collecting the loose, the unregistered, the bright-but-unguarded, the way you'd sweep filings toward a magnet. Your brother is part of the tidying and also, she thinks, doing some of it, his familiar warmth used to make the gathering gentle, a known face to lead the unknown north. 'The Healer,' she says, and the word in her mouth is not a title, it's a diagnosis. 'He doesn't take. He invites. That's why none of your factions have a file thick enough to stop it. You can't arrest an invitation.'

choices.x: Ask her to point you at the next person scheduled to 'wander' north.
choices.hint: Following the next invitation in real time could walk you straight to the gathering point. It means using a stranger as bait on a road you swore would cost no one but you.

choices.x: Ask instead what the gathered ones have in common — find the pattern, not the path.
choices.hint: Understanding who gets invited might tell you why Gin was, and what the Healer is building toward. Pattern is slower than pursuit, and the soup-stall's heater won't keep the trail warm while you think.

choices.x: Show her you trust her — let the fold come loose, just once, just for her to see.
choices.hint: Opening the registers a hair would prove you're truly Gin's and might earn you everything she knows. It is the first crack in the one rule that has kept you human all night, and cracks on this road do not reseal.

beats.scene: Northbound at dawn with no one behind you, and the cost of refusing the fast lanes comes due
prose: Dawn finds you on a Kita-bound platform with the festival burning down to its embers, the lanterns guttering, the dead presumably gone home, and your feet a single continuous ache that has stopped being information and become just the weather of your body. This is the hour the road bills you for everything you refused. A faction would have driven you here. The Gift would have flown you. You walked, and the walking has spent a whole night and most of your strength to bring you only to the edge of the place the others would have started from, and you feel the unfairness of it the way you feel the cold rail under your hands — flatly, without anyone to appeal to. No one is behind you. No procedure protects you. If the thing wearing Gin turns and notices the tired person on the platform, there is no one you can call who will come.

And it does notice — not the way the Gift would be noticed, with the seat's cold eye opening, but in the small, human, deniable way the slow road is haunted: a man across the platform who is reading you a beat too long, a station attendant whose helpfulness has one wrong edge, a sense, unprovable, that the routine you've been tracing has begun, lazily, to trace you back. This is the road's particular dread. It cannot show you a monster, so it shows you the possibility of one in every ordinary face, and leaves you no sight to confirm or dismiss it. You have made yourself into exactly one thing all night — a person asking after Gin — and you are far enough up the line now that asking has become a way of announcing yourself to whatever is doing the gathering.

You could still buy speed, even here, even now. There is always a faster road available to someone desperate enough at dawn — a payphone number the soup-woman slipped you that rings a Grid fixer, a Directorate poster on the platform wall with a tip line that would put a car and a badge behind you within the hour, the simple final option of unfolding your eyes and burning the rest of the distance. The whole night has been a refusal of these, and the refusal has gotten you here intact and unnoticed and nearly out of road. The question the platform asks, while the man across the way folds and unfolds his newspaper, is whether intact and unnoticed is worth the last hour you may have before a lucid window in your brother closes for good.

choices.x: Hold the line — stay slow, stay human, ride the last stretch as just a passenger.
choices.hint: Refuse speed one final time and you arrive the way you set out: unread, unowned, yourself. You may also arrive too late, and spend the rest of your life knowing exactly which trains you let pass.

choices.x: Make the one call — the Grid fixer, a single fast favour at the very end.
choices.hint: One ride from a fixer closes the distance before the window shuts. The Grid never does a favour that doesn't become a handle, and you'd be handing it the thing you walked all night to keep.

choices.x: Confront the man with the newspaper — force the ordinary dread to declare itself.
choices.hint: Making the watcher show his hand ends the not-knowing that's eating you. If he's nothing, you've burned time and nerve; if he's something, you've started a fight with no faction at your back and no sight to fight with.

beats.scene: The fast lane, refused: a CVD junior offers you a car, a badge, and a name to fill in
prose: They come for the unaffiliated last, because the unaffiliated are the hardest to find, and the irony of it nearly makes you laugh as the unmarked car slows beside you on the Kita street and the window comes down on a young CVD officer who is trying very hard to look like help. The Directorate has been watching the gathering too — of course it has, a routine that thins the membrane is exactly the kind of thing it exists to file — and it has noticed, at the very end, the one variable its registries couldn't predict: a sibling tracking the whole pattern on foot, with no faction, no Gift signature, no file. You are, to the young officer's evident discomfort, a blank space in the records that walked itself to the centre of an active case, and the Directorate would very much like to fill the blank in.

The offer is reasonable, which is what makes it dangerous. A car for the last stretch you're too tired to walk. A badge's worth of protection for the threshold you're about to cross unarmed. Resources, backup, the apparatus of a faction that genuinely wants the membrane left alone — all of it yours, in exchange for the one thing the whole night was built to withhold: your brother's name, formally given, on the Directorate's terms, which means Gin stops being a person you're looking for and becomes a person they're processing. The junior officer says the word 'cooperation' and you hear, underneath it, the soft click of a handle being fitted to your brother. Every road but this one began by handing over that handle. You have walked all night precisely to arrive without it, and here, at the last mile, exhaustion makes the case for giving it up better than any officer could.

You look at the young officer and you can see he half hopes you'll refuse — that some part of him knows the difference between a sibling and an informant and would rather not be the one who erases it. The slow road has made you legible to the Directorate in the gentlest possible way, as a witness and not a weapon, and that legibility is itself a kind of door: walk through it and you finish the search with the whole machine behind you and your brother's name in its mouth. Stay on the pavement and you keep faith with the only principle that's gotten you this far, and you keep walking toward the thinning wall with nothing, still, but your own two feet and the warmth of a brother you refuse to spend.

choices.x: Refuse the badge and keep walking — no name, no handle, no faction.
choices.hint: Holding to the road's whole point means arriving at the wall as no one's instrument. It also means facing what's there with a tired body, no backup, and a young officer's car pulling away from the last help you'll be offered.

choices.x: Take the ride but not the deal — accept the car, refuse to give the name.
choices.hint: Bargaining for the distance without paying in Gin's name is the cleverest play available. The Directorate does not give half-favours, and a debt left vague at dawn is a debt they get to define later.

choices.x: Give the officer everything — the routine, the soup-woman's count, the Healer.
choices.hint: Handing the Directorate the full pattern arms the one faction that wants the membrane saved. It also turns every person who helped you tonight into a line in a file, and your brother into a case the machine now owns.

beats.scene: The last streets to the wall, the trail made entirely of small human things
prose: The final approach to the thinning wall is, on this road, the strangest part, because you arrive at it not by sight and not by procedure but by the sheer mass of small things you have carried up the Kita line all night. A clerk's memory of a humming cooler. A cab driver's word for the direction of a calling. A soup-woman's tally of the vanished. A timetable folded to a single stop. Laid end to end, the ordinary facts have become a line as straight and certain as anything the Gift could draw, and you walk it into a quiet northern neighbourhood where the wrongness, when you finally reach it, is not visible at all — it is felt, the way you feel a held breath in a house, the way the dawn light here seems to arrive a half-second late, as if it had to come a little further than light should have to.

You understand, walking these last streets, that the slow road has given you the one thing the fast roads never could: you know how the gathering was done, because you retraced it at the speed it was done at. You know it was gentle. You know it wore a familiar face. You know the people it took were the uncounted, the ones no faction would miss, and you know your brother's warmth was the bait that made the leaving feel like being led home. None of this is sight. All of it is understanding, accumulated on foot, and it has brought you to the threshold with a map of the crime drawn entirely in human testimony — admissible nowhere, true everywhere, and yours alone.

And then, in the late-arriving light, you see him. Not a residue, not a braid of pressures — Gin, your brother, standing at the place where the air comes a half-second late, ordinary as anything, waiting at a thinned wall the way a person waits at a bus stop, his familiar warmth doing the patient work of making a monstrous place look like somewhere it's safe to gather. He has not seen you yet. You have walked all night to be a person finding a person, and here at the end the road has kept its promise exactly: you have found him, with your own tired eyes, paying only in time and shoe leather and the steady refusal to become anything that would have gotten you here faster. The cost was that it took all night. The gift is that you arrive as yourself, unread, with nothing behind you and nothing owed, and a clear human sight of your brother before he turns.

choices.x: Call his name across the quiet street — reach him as a person, out loud.
choices.hint: A voice he's known his whole life might surface the real Gin faster than any power. It also announces you, plainly, to the patient thing wearing him, in the one place it has worked hardest to keep quiet.

choices.x: Watch first — learn what he's doing here before you let yourself be seen.
choices.hint: A few minutes of observation might show you the mechanism of the gathering and how to break it. Every minute is a minute closer to whatever the half-late light is waiting for, and to losing the cover of being unnoticed.

choices.x: Close the distance quietly and put a hand on him before he can turn.
choices.hint: Touch is the most human argument you have, and the hardest for a passenger to answer. Reaching a thinned wall and laying hands on the bait is also exactly the proximity the Healer's whole gentle routine was built to produce.

beats.scene: The threshold, reached by the long way, where being no one is the only card you hold
prose: You arrive at the wall the way only this road could deliver you — with nothing. No badge to flash, no favour to call in, no register flung open to read the seam entire. The other roads converge here too, each handing you a different instrument and a different price already paid; you converge here empty-handed, and for a vertiginous moment the emptiness feels like the failure the whole night was secretly building toward. The membrane has been worked thin in front of you, lovingly, by someone who calls thinning a healing, and you cannot read the plan off it the way the Gift would. You can only stand where your feet have brought you and understand it the slow way: that this is where the gathered ones were gathered, that the vacant Thirteenth Seat is the magnet the soup-woman's filings were swept toward, that your brother's warmth has been the kindness that made a culling feel like a homecoming.

But the road has been building you a different weapon all night, and you feel it now as the last thing it gives you: you are, to the thing on the other side of the wall, illegible. The Gift would have made you the brightest object in northern Tokyo, a flare fired at the opening eye. The factions would have made you a known quantity, a file the Healer could have read in advance. You are neither. You are a tired person who walked here on testimony and stubbornness, carrying no signature anything can lock onto, and at the threshold of a place built to collect the bright and the registered, being no one at all turns out to be the one approach the trap was never designed to catch. The seat's cold attention sweeps the wall and finds nothing to fix on, because you brought nothing for it to fix on, and in that blind spot you are still, impossibly, free to move.

And then his familiar warmth finds you — not flung across a seam by the Gift, but simply Gin, close enough now to feel you the human way, and for one window the size of a held breath the passenger is asleep or distracted or outvoted and it is only your brother, lucid and horrified to see you here. He does not tell you you're too bright; on this road there is no brightness to warn against. He tells you the other thing, the worse and truer thing, in the only language the wall leaves him: that he can't stop walking north, that the kindness in him is being used as bait, that he had hoped no one would ever come the long way and find him doing it. You have found him as yourself, unread, unowned, with nothing behind you and nothing owed — and the only question the wall leaves is what a person with no instrument but their own two hands and their own real face does, now, at the thinned edge of the place their brother is being used to fill.

choices.x: Answer him as his sibling — no plan, no power, just the truth between you.
choices.hint: The one thing the Healer's gentle routine can't counterfeit is the real history between you and Gin. Spent here, at the wall, it might wake the man inside the bait — or it might be the last lucid window you ever get, used up on a conversation instead of a rescue.

choices.x: Stay illegible and try to walk him out the way you walked in — quietly, as nobody.
choices.hint: Leading Gin back down the line as two unremarkable people might slip you both past the seat's blind attention. The thing wearing him does not have to stay asleep, and the long road home is long, and you have no faction to catch you if it wakes.

choices.x: Refuse to take a side at the wall — hold the threshold, change nothing, just stay with him.
choices.hint: Refusing to act, here, keeps every ending still possible and keeps you human to the last. It also leaves the membrane thinning, the seat waiting, and your brother walking north — and someday the not-choosing becomes a choice the city made for you.

sideMissions.title: Yua's Debt
sideMissions.hook: A street kid who watches out for Rei owes the wrong people; the favour she calls in is smaller and worse than money.

beats.scene: Yanaka, the third night of Obon, where the lantern-sellers thin out
prose: Yua finds you the way she always has — not by walking up but by already being there, a smudge of a girl in a man's outgrown jacket leaning on the cold side of a vending machine where the festival light doesn't reach. She is fourteen, or says she is, and she has watched the back of your neck on more platforms than you have ever thanked her for. Tonight the Obon lanterns are going down the Yanaka slope toward the river, paper boats for the dead finding their way home, and she will not look at them. I'm not asking for money, she says before you can offer it, fast, like a thing rehearsed against the chance she'd lose her nerve. Money I could've got. This is the other kind.

You have known for a year that Yua owes someone on the Grid, the way you know a tooth is going bad — by the way she favours one side of every conversation, by the appointments she keeps that she will not name. Now she pulls her sleeve up past the wrist and shows you the underside of her forearm, where there is no mark at all, only skin, and that is the wrong thing, that is the frightening thing: there should be a memory there and there is a smooth absence instead, the place where one has already been lifted clean. I borrowed against remembering, she says. I didn't have anything else worth holding. And the last payment comes due tonight, while the gate's open, because that's when it's cheapest for them and dearest for me.

She tells you the rest in the flat voice children use for the worst things, because feeling it would cost more than she has. The collateral on the final note is the only clear memory she has left of her brother Haru — his actual face, not the photograph she has worn soft, the real grain of his voice telling her something on a train. When the Tallyman collects tonight it comes out of her like a tooth and she will keep the shape of the loss without the thing that was lost. I can't stop it, she says. But you've got two registers you keep stuffed down where they don't show. So I'm asking you to stand there when they take it, and let me tell it to you first — so it's somewhere. So Haru's somewhere. That's the whole favour. It's smaller than money. I know it's worse.

choices.x: "Tell me now, before we go anywhere. I'll hold it."
choices.hint: Taking a memory into a suppressed register isn't free filing — it weights the register, and a register that wakes up on a borrowed grief wakes up loud. You'd be carrying her brother and tipping your own hand at once.

choices.x: "We're not paying it in memory. Take me to whoever holds the note."
choices.hint: The Grid does not renegotiate for sentiment, and a broker who deals in remembering can read what you'd offer instead off the back of your eyes. You'd be walking in with the one currency you can't afford to be seen carrying.

choices.x: "How long until they collect? Don't lie to me about the time."
choices.hint: She has been managing you the way she manages everyone who might help — by the slice. Push for the truth and you'll learn the window is shorter than she let on, and that she came to you last, not first.

beats.scene: Below the Sendagi crossing, where the Grid keeps a night-market the registered city can't see
prose: The Tallyman does not have a face so much as the place where keeping accounts has worn one away. It works a stall under the Sendagi tracks that you would walk past a hundred times registered and never once see, and the moment Yua steps under its awning the festival noise overhead goes muffled, as though the whole bright living city has been folded behind glass. There are jars on its shelves, hundreds, and you make yourself not look too long at any one of them because each holds a little weather of light that moves like something remembering being alive. The watcher girl brings a witness, it says, and its attention crosses your skin like a hand checking a coat for the shape of a wallet. Two of them. One folded twice. How thoughtful, to bring me the interest along with the principal.

It lays the note on the counter the way a doctor lays out an instrument, and the terms are written in Yua's own hand from a year ago, a child's careful characters promising what a child shouldn't have to weigh. The memory of Haru's face, in exchange for the rent she could not make the winter she was eleven. It has been good to her, the Tallyman points out, almost gently — it could have called sooner, on a colder night, for less reason. It is calling now, during Obon, because remembering runs thin when the dead are walking and a memory comes loose easier through the gap, and a debt should be collected at the season that serves the creditor. Unless, it says, and lets the word hang, the witness would prefer to be the payer. I am not particular about whose remembering I file. Only that the ledger closes tonight.

You feel both registers turn over at once, the way a dog lifts its head at a sound under the floor — they have caught the smell of the jars, of so much remembering held still, and they want it. That is the trap inside the trap, and Yua does not know to warn you of it: this is exactly the kind of place that could wake the thing you have spent your whole life keeping asleep. The Tallyman watches you the way it watches everything, as an amount. You came in carrying so much, it says. It would be such a small adjustment, to leave a little lighter.

choices.x: Offer one of your own memories in Haru's place — a thing of yours, freely given.
choices.hint: A clean substitution closes Yua's note and saves Haru's face. But you choose what you offer, and grief makes you reach for the heaviest thing in the room to prove you mean it — and the heaviest thing you own is a morning in a kitchen with Gin, which you cannot afford to lose and may not be able to keep yourself from offering.

choices.x: Refuse the terms and ask what the note would take instead of memory — a service, a name, a debt deferred.
choices.hint: The Tallyman keeps every kind of ledger. It will name a price that isn't memory — and the alternative currencies it deals in are favours owed into the Grid, the same web Gin disappeared through. You'd be trading Yua's grief for a thread that ties you to the thing you're hunting.

choices.x: Let the collection happen, and catch the memory into your register as it comes loose — the favour she actually asked for.
choices.hint: This is the smaller, worse thing she wanted: not rescue, just survival of the memory somewhere. It takes Haru out of her anyway. And the register you open to catch him is one you have never once chosen to open on purpose — you don't know what else comes through the door you hold ajar.

beats.scene: The collection — the instrument set, the gate at its widest
prose: Whatever you decided, the moment of collection is the same shape, and it is quiet, and that is the horror of it — you keep waiting for it to be violent and it is only precise. The Tallyman does not reach for Yua so much as ask the memory a question it cannot help answering, and you watch the girl's face go through something no face should have to do in front of a witness: a brief, terrible brightening, as Haru comes all the way up to the surface one last time to be counted, the real him, laughing at something on a train with the specific crooked tooth the photograph never kept. For one second Yua is eleven and not alone. Then the second ends.

If you reached, you feel him cross — a stranger's brother arriving in a room of yourself you keep dark, the weight of a love you did not earn settling into a register that shudders at the unfamiliar grief and threatens, for one long swimming instant, to open the rest of the way and let out whatever else lives behind it. If you paid, you feel the gap where your own given thing used to be, already smoothing over, already becoming a loss without an edge. If you let it go to close the ledger clean, you watch the brightness leave her and you understand that you chose the cheapest door and that she will know, the way the watched always know about the watcher. The Tallyman files the note and the awning's muffling lifts a half-inch, festival noise leaking back in, the living city remembering it is there.

The ledger is closed, it says, and it is already looking past both of you at the next set of footsteps in the dark. But it pauses, because it deals in what people will give and it has taken your measure now and found it useful to know. You hold a great deal you have not counted, it tells you, not unkindly, the way a creditor is kind to a client it intends to see again. When you are ready to know the true sum of yourself, you know which stall keeps the longest ledger in the city. Bring the watcher girl. She remembers where the door is, even when she cannot remember why.

choices.x: Get Yua out into the lantern-light before you let yourself feel any of it.
choices.hint: She is fourteen and she has just lost the last real piece of someone, in public, in front of you. Putting her first is right — and it means you carry whatever just happened to you, alone, unexamined, into a register you can't be sure is closed again.

choices.x: Tell the Tallyman you'll be back to learn the true sum — and mean it.
choices.hint: It is the first creature in the city to offer you a straight account of what you actually are. That is a door you have wanted your whole life. It is also a hook, set by a thing that does nothing without a ledger, in the exact season your brother went looking through a gap like this one.

choices.x: Say nothing. Pick up a lantern from the stack and put it in Yua's hands.
choices.hint: A boat for a brother she can no longer picture. The gesture costs nothing and means everything, which is the only kind of payment left tonight — and it tells her you understood exactly what you witnessed, which is its own weight to have laid on a child.

beats.scene: The river stairs, after — paper boats going down toward a sea none of them will reach
prose: You take her down to the water where the others are launching their lanterns, and Yua kneels at the bottom step with the paper boat you put in her hands, and for a while she cannot light it because she has forgotten who it is for. That is the part the Tallyman charged her for and did not bother to mention: not the memory only but the why of keeping it, so that she holds a grief with the name scraped off, a love with no object, the worst kind of debt because it cannot be discharged by remembering or forgotten by trying. It was somebody, she says, testing the words. It was somebody good. I can feel the shape of good. I just can't get the rest to come. And you, who chose tonight whether to carry her brother or your own kitchen or nothing at all, sit down on the cold stone beside her and do not lie about how that feels.

If you took Haru into your register, you find you can give a little of him back — not the memory, you cannot return what the ledger took, but the fact of him, the train and the tooth and the laugh, told as a witness tells a thing, so that she has a story where she used to have the man. It is not the same and it is not nothing, and she listens to her own brother described by a stranger with a hunger that breaks something in you that you did not know was load-bearing. If you paid instead, you discover the cost only now — reaching for the thing you gave and finding the smooth place where it was, learning by its absence how much you must have loved it. If you let the collection close clean, the silence between you on the steps is honest, at least, and she does not pretend you saved her, and you do not pretend you tried.

When the boat finally goes down — and it does, all of them do, the whole grieving city pushing its dead gently out toward a darkness that is, tonight, briefly thin — Yua watches it until the current takes it round the bend and then she stands, and she is fourteen again, and the watching is already back in her, the appraisal of exits and angles that has kept her alive. You'll go looking for your one too, she says, not asking, because she has watched the back of your neck for a year and she knows the shape of a person hunting a brother through a gap in the world. When you do — don't borrow against the remembering. Whatever they offer. That's the favour back. And she is gone up the slope into the lantern-light before you can tell her it is already, probably, too late for that advice, and that the longest ledger in the city has your measure now, and that you came down here carrying one more thing than you arrived with, and you have not yet dared to count it.

choices.x: Promise her you won't borrow against remembering — knowing what you're already carrying.
choices.hint: A promise to a child you may not be able to keep, made in a city where your brother's whole disappearance runs through favours owed into the dark. She'll hold you to it. So will you.

choices.x: Go back up the slope toward the Grid market, tonight, while the door is open.
choices.hint: The Tallyman offered you the true sum of yourself, and Gin went looking through a gap exactly like this one. Walking back in now means following him into the same dark by the same light — and you'd be doing it alone, with a register you opened tonight and can't swear is shut.

choices.x: Let her go, and sit with what you carried out, and finally count it.
choices.hint: The thing you've avoided all night. Whatever you took on at the stall — Haru's grief, the gap where your own gift was, or the cheap clean nothing — you face it here on the stone, where there's no one left to manage and no festival noise loud enough to drown it out.

sideMissions.title: The Thing in the Dorm
sideMissions.hook: Mori's crush is the least of it; something has moved into the third-floor washroom and only he can see it.

beats.scene: Outside the Nezu prep-school dormitory, the fourth night of Obon, where a boy is standing who should be inside asleep
prose: Mori is waiting under the dormitory's dead entrance light, hands jammed in the pockets of a uniform he no longer has any daytime reason to be wearing — the summer term ended a week ago and most of the building has gone home to the provinces to meet its dead. He is seventeen and he has the specific carefulness of a boy who has decided, somewhere on the long walk to find you, exactly which words he will use and in which order, and he loses the order the instant he sees you. I didn't know who else, he starts, and stops, and the blush that climbs his neck is the small ordinary trouble, the crush he carries for you that you have always handled the way you'd handle something breakable left in your care — gently, plainly, without ever once making it a joke. It's not — this isn't about that. I need you to believe me about something and you're the only person I know who won't tell me I'm sick.

It is in the third-floor washroom, he says, and the moment he says it the carefulness goes out of him and the real thing underneath shows through, which is that he has not slept properly in four nights and has been washing at the kitchen tap downstairs because he cannot make himself walk past that door. Something moved in two nights before Obon opened. At first it was only that the long mirror over the end sink held the room a half-second behind the room, the way a tired eye lags — and then it was that the water standing in the blocked third basin showed someone bending over it when no one was, and now, he tells you, looking at his own shoes, now it has a face it is still deciding on, and the face it is deciding on is getting closer to his every night. Nobody else sees it, he says. I made Tanaka stand in there with me for an hour and he saw a dripping tap and a kid losing it. But you — you see things. I've watched you not-look at things on the platform the exact way I've started not-looking at that mirror.

You feel both registers turn over once, low, the way a house settles — not at Mori, who is only frightened, but at the thing behind what he is describing, because a presence that copies the room a half-second late and wears slowly toward a watcher's face is a known and patient shape, and Obon is the season it does its best work. The membrane is thin all week; the dead are abroad and the living are gentle and distracted and easy to read, and into that softness things that are not dead and not alive find it cheap to move in and set up housekeeping. You could tell him it is nothing. You have told kinder lies. But he has watched the back of your neck the way the watched always learn to watch, and he would know.

choices.x: "Take me up there now, while the gate's still open. I want to see it deciding."
choices.hint: A thing is most readable while it's still forming and most dangerous for the same reason — it hasn't chosen what it is, so it will try anything on, including you. Going up tonight means meeting it before it's finished, which is also before you know what it can do.

choices.x: "Tell me exactly what the face looks like now. Don't soften it."
choices.hint: He'll describe the half-built thing in the mirror and you'll recognise the architecture: it isn't deciding on a random face. It's wearing toward his — and a copy that finishes a face can wear it out the door, in a building where no one's home to notice the boy was replaced.

choices.x: "You're not sleeping in this building tonight. I'll go up alone."
choices.hint: Protecting him is right and it's also exactly wrong: the thing has spent four nights keyed to Mori specifically, learning him, and if you take the original away while you walk into its room, you give it the one night it needs to finish from memory — and a finished copy doesn't need the boy present to become him.

beats.scene: The third-floor washroom, past two in the morning, the building emptied for the festival of the dead
prose: The corridor up to the third floor is the worst kind of quiet, the quiet of a place built to hold a hundred sleeping bodies and holding none — every door propped open on a bare mattress and a square of streetlight, the air still carrying the ghost of a hundred deodorants and instant-noodle steam with no one left to make more. The washroom door is the only one shut. Mori stops a body-length short of it and you understand that this is as far as he has been able to come for four nights, that he has stood exactly here and turned around exactly here, and that walking you the rest of the way is the bravest thing he will do tonight and possibly the most foolish. You push the door. The fluorescent tube inside is already on, humming, though no one has been up here to switch it, and that is the first wrong thing, the small administrative impossibility that tells you the room has started keeping its own hours.

The basins run along the left wall under a single long mirror gone soft at the silvering, and the third basin from the end is blocked, holding a hand's depth of standing water that should have drained days ago and instead sits perfectly still and faintly warm, you can feel the warmth of it from the door like the breath off a sleeping animal. The mirror holds the room. Then, as you watch, it holds the room a half-second behind — your own reflection raising its eyes a beat after you raise yours, Mori's reflection flinching a beat after Mori does — and in the standing water of the third basin there is a face looking up that is not a reflection of anything in the room, a face caught at the stage a drawing reaches when the artist has the shape and is still working the features, and the features it is working are Mori's. It's more done than last night, Mori whispers behind you, and his voice cracks straight down the middle. That's — those are my eyes. It didn't have my eyes yesterday.

Your registers are fully awake now and straining toward the basin the way they strained toward the Tallyman's jars, because here is the same forbidden sweetness — a thing made entirely of held attention, of being looked at, and to read it you would have to look, and looking is what feeds it. It knows you are there. The unfinished Mori in the water tilts its half-made head with a curiosity that is precisely, horribly, the gesture you have seen the real boy make, and the standing water does not ripple, and the mirror gives up pretending to be a half-second slow and simply stops, holding a still image of the room while the room keeps moving, so that you are looking at a photograph of a place you are standing in. The fluorescent tube hums on, patient as a held breath.

choices.x: Look directly into the standing water and read what's forming there.
choices.hint: Reading it would tell you what it is and how nearly finished — and it feeds on exactly the act of being looked at. Your sight thins the veil wherever you turn it; turning it on a thing that grows under attention is pouring water on the root to see how thirsty it is.

choices.x: Pull the plug on the third basin and break the standing water before it sets.
choices.hint: Deny it the still pool and you take away one of its two windows — but the thing isn't in the water, it's using the water, and you don't yet know if breaking its medium scatters it or simply drives the unfinished copy fully into the mirror, where it's a half-second from done.

choices.x: Put yourself bodily between Mori and the glass and don't let him be looked at.
choices.hint: Blocking its line to the original starves the copy of fresh detail — and stands you, with your two unguarded registers, directly in the gaze of a thing that wears whoever it watches longest. You'd be trading a near-finished Mori for a fresh start on you.

beats.scene: The thing chooses what to offer — and offers the one thing the boy can't easily refuse
prose: Whatever you did, the room answers, and the answer is not a lunge or a scream but a courtesy, which is so much worse. The half-made Mori in the water finishes a fraction more — finds the rest of its eyes, its mouth — and it does not look at you at all. It looks at the real Mori, past your shoulder, with an expression of such uncomplicated welcome that you feel the boy behind you go still, and you realise the thing is not threatening him. It is inviting him. The fluorescent light warms by a degree and the mirror, which had frozen, begins very gently to show a different room than the one you are in: the same washroom but in some softened later evening, and in it Mori is laughing at something, and beside Mori, turned toward him, listening, choosing to be there, is you. That's not real, Mori says, but he says it the way you say a thing you are arguing yourself out of, and his voice has gone young.

You understand the mechanism now and it turns your stomach with how reasonable it is. The thing does not steal a face by force; it grows one out of wanting, and it has spent four nights learning that the strongest, most constant wanting in this boy is the small impossible wish that you would stay, that the kindness you show him would tip one degree over into the thing he doesn't let himself name. It cannot make that true. So it makes a room where it looks true, and it wears his face toward him as an open door, and all it needs — all a copy ever needs to finish and to walk — is for the original to look at the version of himself who gets the thing he wants, and to want, for one unguarded second, to be him instead. In a building emptied for Obon, a finished Mori could leave by the front door at dawn and meet his returning roommates as himself, and the real boy would be the depth of water in a blocked basin, draining slowly, unmissed for days.

And you feel, underneath your alarm, the colder private recognition that this is your own oldest fear wearing a stranger's size — a thing that reads what you most want and builds a door out of it, that takes a person by being more them than they can bear to refuse. Somewhere across the thinning city your brother went through a gap like this one and something came back wearing the shape of him, the Healer in Gin's worn coat, and here in a student washroom is the same crime in miniature, patient, almost gentle, asking only that the boy agree to be replaced by the better version of his own loneliness. The unfinished Mori in the glass holds out the evening where you stay. It is waiting, with infinite courtesy, for someone to say yes.

choices.x: Make Mori say it out loud — that the boy in the glass isn't him, and the evening isn't real, and he doesn't want it enough to vanish for it.
choices.hint: A copy grown from wanting starves the instant the original refuses to want it — but you'd be asking a seventeen-year-old to stand in front of you and renounce, aloud, the one wish he's never said, while you watch. The cure is making him say the quiet thing to your face. It'll cost him something he doesn't get back.

choices.x: Offer yourself to its gaze instead — turn your two registers full on it and let it try to copy the richer meal.
choices.hint: Pull it off the boy and onto you and Mori is safe tonight. But you carry two suppressed registers and a morning in a kitchen you'd die before losing, and a thing that wears whoever it watches longest has just been handed the most detailed person in the building — and you don't know if you can outlast its attention.

choices.x: Refuse to look at the offered evening at all, and instead read the thing for what it actually is — its name, its hunger, its weakness.
choices.hint: Knowing what it is lets you end it properly instead of only chasing it off — but reading is looking, and looking feeds it, and the longer you study the architecture of a thing built to be the thing you want, the longer it has to study the architecture of you.

beats.scene: The unmaking — done quietly, in fluorescent light, while the dead walk outside
prose: The breaking, when it comes, is as quiet as the Tallyman's collection and runs the opposite direction — not a thing taken out of someone but a thing refused entry, which the body experiences, strangely, as grief. If you made Mori speak, he does it badly and truly, his voice shaking, telling the boy in the glass you're not me, I don't want it like that, I'd rather be lonely and real than that and gone, and you watch the cruelty of asking it land on his face even as it works — the half-made copy loses its eyes first, the eyes it stole last, because an unwanted thing cannot keep the parts that were only ever made of wanting. If you offered yourself, you feel it turn on you with a hunger that nearly takes your knees, your registers flaring toward the mirror with their own terrible willingness, and you learn how close to the surface they have always been by how hard you have to fight to keep your own face your own. If you read it, you find its small true name — a left-behind, a thing that was once a reflection that someone looked at too long in grief and never released — and naming it is a kind of mercy and a kind of murder at once.

The standing water in the third basin goes cold all at once, the warmth leaving it like a held breath finally let go, and the unfinished Mori comes apart not violently but the way a face comes apart in disturbed water, features sliding off the surface tension and sinking, and the mirror gives a long shudder and shows, for one plain second, only the actual room — two real people, badly frightened, alive — before it goes back to being ordinary soft-silvered glass that lags not at all. The fluorescent tube stutters and resumes its honest indifferent hum. It is over so undramatically that Mori makes a sound that is half a sob and half a laugh, the sound of a body discovering it is still its own. And you stand there with your registers slowly settling, knowing what you now know: that the difference between this washroom and your brother's disappearance is only one of scale and patience, and that the thing wearing Gin across the city did not finish in four nights and was not refused in time.

There is a residue. There is always a residue. A thread of the thing's attention has not gone down with the rest — you can feel it the way you feel a draft from a door not quite latched, somewhere up near the silvering of the long mirror, thinned to almost nothing but not nothing, the way a copy keeps the memory of a face even after the face is taken back. Whether it can grow again before the gate closes at the end of Obon, you cannot say. What you can say is that it has Mori's measure and a little of yours, and that things made of wanting do not forget where the wanting lives.

choices.x: Hold Mori up — he's a boy who just renounced his own loneliest wish and his legs don't know it's over yet.
choices.hint: He needs a hand on his shoulder and a real human weight to come back to. Giving it is simple and right. It also means he feels, through your steadiness, exactly how unshaken you are by horrors that flattened him — and he files that, the way the watched file everything, and wonders what you've already survived to be this calm.

choices.x: Reach up and take the thread of residue into a register, to study what a left-behind is made of.
choices.hint: It's the same greed the Tallyman read in you — the wish to know the true architecture of the thing that nearly wore a boy, because something is wearing your brother and you are starving for the mechanism. But you'd be carrying a live splinter of a copy-thing in a register you can't swear stays shut.

choices.x: Salt the basins, drain the third, and do the small Obon rite over the mirror to send the left-behind out with the proper dead.
choices.hint: The clean way, the slow way, the way that closes the door instead of only shutting it — and it means staying in this room another hour past your own fear, doing folk-work with cold hands, on the chance that a residue you could almost ignore comes back wearing the boy you just saved.

beats.scene: Dawn at the dormitory gate — the first morning Mori has walked past a mirror in four days
prose: You bring him down through the waking building as the streetlights click off one by one, and at the gate the early Obon quiet has that washed, forgiven quality the city only has at this hour in this week, the pavement still cool, a single lantern-seller down the block setting out paper boats for the evening's launch. Mori has stopped shaking. He has the loose, scoured lightness of someone who has been afraid for so long that the absence of fear feels almost like floating, and he keeps testing it, glancing at the dark window-glass of the parked cars and finding only himself in them, an ordinary tired seventeen-year-old, lagging not at all. It really showed you, he says eventually, not looking at you, meaning the evening in the mirror, meaning the thing he had to say out loud to make it die. I'm sorry you had to see what it — what I— and he cannot finish, and the blush is back, the small ordinary trouble surfacing now that the enormous one has drained away.

So you handle it the way you have always handled it, plainly, without making it small. You tell him that the thing did not invent his wish, it only found it and wore it, and that there is nothing in him to be ashamed of for having wanted to be chosen, because wanting to be chosen is the most human thing there is and not a weakness a thing can be blamed for exploiting. And you tell him the true part, the part that costs you a little to say and costs him more to hear and is the only thing worth saying: that you are not the evening in the glass and were never going to be, that what is between you is real and is friendship and is not a lesser thing for being that, and that he stood in a room and refused a false version of you to keep the true one, which is the bravest and most adult thing you have watched anyone do all week. He nods. He understands. It will sit in him for a while and then it will settle into something good, and he will be, you think, all right.

What you do not tell him is the rest — that you walked into his washroom hunting the mechanism of your own grief and found it running in miniature, a patient thing that reads what a person most wants and builds a door out of it and waits, with infinite courtesy, to walk out wearing them. That something across the city did exactly this to your brother and was not made to say the true thing out loud in time. That you felt your own two registers strain toward the glass with a willingness that frightened you more than the copy did, because it means you, too, are a thing that could be worn, a door someone is already standing patiently outside of. Down the block the lantern-seller lights the first of the day's paper boats, and Mori watches it the way you both watched the basin — carefully, from a body-length back — and asks, in a small voice, whether the thing is really gone. You tell him the truth, which is that you closed the door, and that doors in this season do not always stay closed, and that you will check the washroom every night until the gate shuts and the dead go home. It is the most honest comfort you have. He takes it. The morning comes up over the dormitory roof, indifferent and clean, and for now there is only one of each of you, which is, this week, a great deal to be able to say.

choices.x: Tell him the truth about why you came up there — that you know exactly what it is to be hunted for your face.
choices.hint: It would mean something to him to know he wasn't a charity case, that you needed that room as much as he did. It would also hand a frightened seventeen-year-old the knowledge that the person he trusts most is being stalked by a bigger version of what nearly ate him — and you can't take that back once he's carrying it.

choices.x: Promise to check the washroom every night until the gate closes — and keep the promise.
choices.hint: The residue up in the silvering isn't nothing, and a left-behind grows where the wanting lives, and Mori's wanting hasn't gone anywhere just because he said the words once. Keeping the promise ties you to this dormitory for the rest of Obon, the same nights your brother's trail is thinning fastest across the city.

choices.x: Walk him to the river and put a lantern in his hands for the self he refused to become.
choices.hint: A boat for the boy in the glass who got the evening — grieving, properly, the false future he gave up so the true one could stay real. It's the right rite and it costs nothing but the admission, made beside a child, that you have your own such boat to launch and have not yet found the nerve to light it.

sideMissions.title: Tanizaki's Drowned Client
sideMissions.hook: A Grid fixer wants a body found before the river gives it up on its own terms.

beats.scene: Tanizaki's back room above the shuttered tea shop, the second afternoon of Obon, rain not yet arrived but promised
prose: Tanizaki pours before he speaks, which is how you know the matter is serious — the old man has spent forty years in Kita learning that nothing true gets said over an empty cup, and he has never once wasted the gesture on small business. The room smells of roasted barley and the river two streets over, that brown August smell of low tide and lantern-wax that the whole district wears this week, and through the rice-paper the light has gone the colour of weak tea itself, flat and waiting. He sets your cup down with both hands and folds his own around his and says, without preamble, that a man went into the Sumida three nights ago and has not come up, and that this is not a police matter and is not going to become one, and that he needs the man found before the river gives him up on its own terms.

You let him talk. The drowned man's name was Kase — a fixer, Grid-side, the kind of careful unregistered go-between who arranges that a thing change hands without either hand being seen, and Tanizaki had used him for thirty years the way you use a tool you trust enough to stop noticing. Three nights ago Kase sent word he had something that had frightened him, something he wanted off his hands and into Tanizaki's before Obon's gate opened all the way, and then he sent nothing, and then a Grid courier found his flat aired and empty with the kettle still warm and his shoes by the door. A man does not walk to the river barefoot in this season by accident, Tanizaki says, and turns his cup a quarter-turn on the table, and does not drink. And the Sumida in Obon does not keep what it takes the ordinary way. It launches the dead all week. I would rather find Kase before the river decides he is one of them.

Both registers move at that, low, the way they move when something true is being undersold — because Tanizaki is not asking you to recover a body, not really, he is asking you to read one, and he knows what reading a drowned man this week will pull through you and is asking anyway, which is itself a measure of his fear. You have known the old man as the one person in Kita who never spends you carelessly, who shaped your brother's whole field practice with exactly this restraint, and to watch him push a cup toward you with a thing he wants kept off the official ledger is to understand that whatever Kase was carrying, it reaches further than one fixer's bad night by the water. The rain has not started. Outside, somewhere down toward the embankment, the first of the evening's lantern-sellers begins setting out paper boats no one has yet died recently enough to need.

choices.x: "What was he carrying that frightened him? Tell me before I go near the water."
choices.hint: Tanizaki will tell you as much as he knows, which is little and pointed — and knowing what Kase held means you'll be reading the river for it too, not just for a body. The more precisely you know what you're hunting, the more precisely it can be hunting back through the same thinned water.

choices.x: "Why keep it off the police book? A drowning in Obon is the most ordinary thing in Tokyo."
choices.hint: His answer will tell you who else is interested in Kase's last errand and why a clean municipal recovery would be the wrong kind of clean. But pressing the old man on why he wants it quiet invites him to tell you exactly how far up the obligation runs — and once you know, you're inside it.

choices.x: Say nothing; drink the tea, take the address of Kase's flat, and go to the water cold.
choices.hint: Going in without the frame keeps your reading uncontaminated by what Tanizaki expects you to find — you'll see only what the river shows. It also means meeting whatever held a careful man under, with no idea what it wanted from him or what it might recognise in you.

beats.scene: The Sumida embankment after dark, downstream of Kase's flat, the first lanterns going onto the water
prose: The river at this hour is a black road carrying small fires. Toro nagashi has begun upstream and the lanterns come down in loose constellations, paper boxes each with a candle and a name brushed on the side, the families' grief made buoyant and sent out to float the dead home across the dark — and you stand on the concrete embankment where the city's romance about the river ends and its plumbing begins, smelling diesel and silt, watching the little lights come on past you toward the bay. This is the worst place to use your sight and you came here to use it. The membrane is at its thinnest all week and nowhere thinner than over running water at the festival of the dead, and the moment you let the first register open a hand's width the whole surface of the Sumida tilts in your perception from a river with lanterns on it to a procession, a long patient column of the departing moving with the current, and every paper flame is suddenly attended.

You walk the embankment downstream, reading for the wrong note in a song of the dead — and a drowned man three nights gone is a wrong note, because the properly dead this week are leaving and Kase is not leaving, Kase is held. You feel him before you see anything, the way you feel a snag in cloth, somewhere down past the third pier where the current goes slack behind a concrete footing and the lanterns that drift in there turn slow circles and do not come out. The held place has a temperature your sight reads as cold and your skin reads as nothing at all. Down there, in the slack water behind the pier, something keeps a man the way the third basin kept a half-made boy — not eating him, not yet, just holding, the way you hold a thing you have not decided whether to use.

And here is the part Tanizaki could not have prepared you for, the part both registers strain toward with their old forbidden appetite: the held place is not silent. It is leaking. A drowned man read this fresh, this snagged, still has his last quarter-hour in him the way a struck bell holds its note, and you can feel Kase's final minutes pressing out against the river's grip — the cold, the weight of his own coat, a decision, a hand that was or was not on the back of his neck — all of it down there waiting to be looked at, and looking is exactly what thins the wall, and the wall over this slack water is already thin enough to put your fingers through. The lanterns turn their slow circles behind the pier. One of them, you notice, has no name brushed on its side at all.

choices.x: Open the register fully and read the slack water from the bank, before you go down to it.
choices.hint: Reading from a distance tells you what's holding Kase and how, so you go down knowing — but opening fully over running water during Obon is putting your hand through the thinnest membrane in the city, and a thing that holds the drowned will feel the warm living attention arrive and turn, unhurried, to see what's looking.

choices.x: Climb down to the slack water and find the body with your hands, registers shut, sight ordinary.
choices.hint: Going in blind keeps your sight off the membrane and denies the held thing the meal of your attention — but it means lowering yourself into cold slack water in the dark to feel for a three-day drowning by touch, with whatever kept him circling somewhere you can't see, and trusting your hands to know a held man from a held thing.

choices.x: Pull the nameless lantern out of the slack water first and read it instead of the man.
choices.hint: A lantern with no name that won't leave the held place isn't a stranger's grief gone astray — it's bait, or a marker, or Kase's own, and reading it might tell you who put him there without making you look at the body at all. But taking the thing the held place is keeping is the same as knocking, and it will answer.

beats.scene: Behind the third pier, knee-deep in slack water, the moment the river gives Kase up
prose: He is where you knew he was, hung in the slack behind the footing with one sleeve snagged on rebar and the rest of him turning slow in the eddy, face down, coat heavy as a drowned animal — and the river, when you take his wrist, does not fight you for him the way you braced for. It gives him up. That is the first wrong thing and the worst: a body three nights held in slack water should be claimed, should be the river's, and instead the current eases its grip the instant you commit to taking him, the way a thing hands you something it wanted you to have all along. You turn him over in the dark and the lantern-light from upstream slides across a face that drowning has been gentle with, slack and almost untroubled, a careful man who at the very end stopped being careful — and the last quarter-hour, freed by your touch, comes off him into your open register like cold off a stone.

You read it because you cannot not, and it is not what Tanizaki sold you. Kase did not slip. Kase walked here barefoot in the dark with the thing that frightened him buttoned into his coat, because the thing that frightened him was a name — a list, a small waxed-paper ledger of who in Kita had taken a particular favour in the last two years and what each favour had quietly cost the membrane to grant — and Kase had understood, three nights too late, that to carry such a list was to be a loose thread in something very large and very patient, and that the only place in the city thin enough to lose it where no register could read it again was the bottom of the Sumida in Obon. He did not drown himself out of fear. He drowned himself to hide the ledger somewhere even the dead could not be made to give it up, and he walked in barefoot and unhurried, and the river, this week, was glad to keep them both.

And the held thing is here, of course it is here, you have felt it the whole time the way you feel a watcher behind glass — not a demon and not a ghost but the slack place itself gone aware, a stretch of Obon river that has held a hidden man and a hidden name for three nights and learned, the way standing water learns, the taste of being a secret-keeper. It does not want Kase. It wants the going-on of it, the warm thing now kneeling in its water with two registers open and a brother across the city it can feel you ache toward — and it offers, in the wordless slack-water way, to hold for you too, to take whatever you most need hidden and keep it at the bottom where no Healer and no Directorate and no patient brother-shaped thing could ever read it off you. The ledger is buttoned cold against the dead man's chest. The nameless lantern turns its slow circle by your knee. The current waits to see what you do with all three.

choices.x: Take the ledger off the body — Kishin would kill for who-owes-what in Kita, and so would the people on it.
choices.hint: The waxed list is the single most valuable object you've touched all week: a map of every quiet favour and its membrane-cost, which is a map straight toward what Yushiro is doing to your brother. Carrying it out of the river makes you the loose thread Kase died to cut — and the slack place will remember exactly who took the secret it was keeping.

choices.x: Leave the ledger where the dead man drowned to hide it, and bring up only Kase.
choices.hint: Honouring a man's last terrible decision means giving Tanizaki a body and no answers, and leaving the one document that might explain your brother at the bottom of a river you'd have to read again to recover. It's the clean grief and the coward's mercy at once, and you'll never be sure which.

choices.x: Let the slack water make its offer real — give it one thing of yours to hold while you decide.
choices.hint: The river is offering the safest hiding place in Tokyo for the one truth you can't afford anyone to read off you, and the relief of it is enormous and immediate. It is also exactly how it took Kase: one careful man's reasonable wish to hide a single thing, and a patient water glad to keep the man along with it.

beats.scene: On the embankment again, soaked, the body laid out under a tarp, deciding what the river is allowed to keep
prose: You get him out — that much you do not let yourself negotiate — and lay Kase on the concrete above the tide-line under a courier's tarp Tanizaki's network leaves cached for exactly such nights, and you kneel there dripping while the lanterns keep coming down past the pier, indifferent, name after name floating out toward a sea that does not read. Whatever you carried up the bank with you sits heavy and cold against your own chest or sits at the bottom where Kase put it, and either way you have made the choice that the rest of this week will be lived inside. The slack water behind the footing has gone ordinary again, just river, the awareness in it lapsed back into mere current the moment it got — or did not get — what it offered to hold, and you understand that you will not be able to tell anyone the difference between the version where you outwitted it and the version where you simply weren't worth keeping.

There is the matter of the body, which is also the matter of the truth. A barefoot drowning in Obon is the most ordinary death in Tokyo and the most explicable, and you could hand Kase to the morning and the municipal book and let him be a sad seasonal statistic, the river's romance intact, no one the wiser about waxed ledgers or favours that cost the wall. Or you could give him the rite he chose for himself — slide him back to the proper dead with a lantern and a name, let the festival carry out a man who walked into it on purpose — and keep his death off every book, which is what Tanizaki asked and what Kase died to arrange. The rain has finally started, fine and warm, dimpling the black water and guttering the nearer candles, and the dead go on leaving regardless, and you have to decide whose terms Kase departs on: the river's, the city's, or his own.

Both registers are still half-open and slow to close, the way they always are after running water, and through them you feel the shape of what you've actually been doing down here, which is not a favour for an old man at all. You came to the Sumida to practise the unbearable thing — to read a held person whom a patient power did not want to release, to take or refuse a hidden truth, to sit knee-deep in a thinned place and not be kept — because somewhere across the city your brother is held exactly so, in slack water of a different kind, by a Healer glad to keep him, and you do not yet have the nerve or the method to go in after him. Kase was rehearsal. The knowledge sits in you cold as the river: that you could find Gin, perhaps, the way you found this man, and that finding is the easy half, and that the water does not always give up what you commit to taking.

choices.x: Launch Kase yourself — a lantern, his name, the proper rite, his death off every book.
choices.hint: Giving him the departure he chose honours a brave and terrible decision and keeps Tanizaki's promise of silence. It also means you, personally, perform the rite to send a man out with the dead this week — and standing over the water saying the words for someone else's chosen drowning teaches your hands how it would be done for one you love.

choices.x: Call it in clean — let Kase be an ordinary Obon drowning on the municipal book, truth buried with the routine.
choices.hint: The official version protects you and everyone on the ledger by making the death boring, which is the safest thing a death can be. But it spends Tanizaki's trust, brands you to the Grid as someone who hands their dead to the authorities, and lets the city's lie about the river stand over a man who died telling the truth about it.

choices.x: Bring Kase and what he carried straight to Tanizaki and put the whole choice in the old man's hands.
choices.hint: Tanizaki has forty years of judgement you don't, and he loved Kase in his restrained way, and the decision is arguably his to make. Handing it up also hands him the ledger — and you'll have learned nothing about whether you can carry such a weight alone, the night before the week demands you carry a heavier one.
